fields.description: Optimization: The radius of a theoretical bounding sphere after which the light cuts off. This is a quick cutoff but not a sharp one to prevent being confused with a bug. This further attenuates physically-correct intensity falloff. The intent is to allow tight bounds on lights that otherwise would cover a great area with minimal contribution. In general a light should be authored with this at zero (default value) or a very large number so it does not influence the physically-correct falloff, then radius should be walked back to the smallest value where no difference is practically noticed. See Cutoff Dist, which is a hard end-of-influence bound that by-design causes lighting to stop with no graceful falloff. If Attenuation Radius is larger than Cutoff Dist, this continuity will become evident.
fields.label: Light Attenuation Radius

fields.description: This is the heightfield texture asset that will be used with this piece of terrain.  It should be a 16-bit single-channel texture representing the height.  Note that the height will range from 0.0 to 1.0, and the terrain instance's matrix will take care of putting that in world space.

fields.description: This is the texture asset that will be used for heightfield painting.  This is a texture array where the first layer (the 'Source File' field) is the painted data and the subsequent (optional) layers contains heightfields created by a DCC tool.  For heightfields created by DCC tools, the height should range from 0.0 to 1.0.  If no DCC heighfield is specified, a heightfield with a value of 0.0 is assumed.  The paint layer should also range from 0.0 to 1.0; however, it will lower the height of the DCC-generated heightfields if the value is less than 0.5, and raise the height of the DCC-generated heightfields if the value is greater than 0.5.  Because the paint layer can raise or lower values, the vertical granularity is halved.
fields.label: HeightField Paint
fields.name: HeightFieldPaint

fields.description: This is the splatmask texture asset that will be used with this piece of terrain.  It should be a standard RGBA texture.
fields.label: NONE
fields.name: SplatMask

fields.description: This is the texture asset that will be used for splatmask painting.  This is a texture array where the first layer (the 'Source File' field) is the painted data and the second (optional) layer contains a splatmask created by a DCC tool.  For splatmasks created by DCC tools, the RGBA values should range from 0.0 to 1.0.  If no DCC splatmask is specified, a splatmask with a value of (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) is assumed.  The paint layer should also range from 0.0 to 1.0; however, it will lower the height of the DCC-generated splatmasks if the value is less than 0.5, and raise the height of the DCC-generated heightfields if the value is greater than 0.5.  Because the paint layer can raise or lower values, the vertical granularity is halved.

fields.description:
Should we always cast shadows, never cast shadows, or dissolve shadows normally using the pre-shader?
Whether or not shadows are cast is based on these rules:

1. If a shader wants to disable shadows completely, shadows will be disabled regardless of the other shaders' values.

2. If no shader wants shadows disabled completely, but a shader wants to always cast shadows, complete shadows will be cast.

fields.description: Optimization: The radius of a theoretical bounding sphere after which the light cuts off. This is a quick cutoff but not a sharp one to prevent being confused with a bug. This further attenuates physically-correct intensity falloff. The intent is to allow tight bounds on lights that otherwise would cover a great area with minimal contribution. In general a light should be authored with this at zero (default value) or a very large number so it does not influence the physically-correct falloff, then radius should be walked back to the smallest value where no difference is practically noticed. See Cutoff Dist, which is a hard end-of-influence bound that by-design causes lighting to stop with no graceful falloff. If Attenuation Radius is larger than Cutoff Dist, this continuity will become evident.

fields.label: Cast Shadows
fields.name: CastShadows

fields.description:
No Shadows: The light casts no shadows, no geometry will occlude this light.
Cache Static Models: Default behavior. When the light isn't animating, all static casters are cached for performance.
Only Static Models: Cheap option for placed lights. Static models will cast shadows but dynamic ones won't. On most frames no work needs to be done to render the shadow map.
Only Dynamic Models: Useful for optimizing cinematic lighting when you only care about the shadows from the actors in the shot.
fields.label: Shadow Cast Type
fields.name: ShadowCastType

fields.description:
Optimization: Higher resolutions gain detail, however have a higher fill-rate performance cost. Regardless of the setting, shadow res reduces further into the distance. If this setting is insufficient, check the following:
Scene Light Count If there are more shadowing lights than memory can bear, all shadows will be downres'ed until all fit.
Light Angle A shadow map must cover the entirety of the lit area, so wide angles on spot lights, or point lights that affect a great area will see their effective shadow resolution decrease as it's spread thinner over a greater area.
Note: Point lights actually generate 6 shadow maps, one for each cardinal axis direction/face of a cube, so they are 6x the cost of a spot light in terms of shadow cost.
fields.label: NONE
fields.name: ShadowRes

fields.description: Non-PBR aesthetic tweak This is intended to allow for fine control of spec response, especially in cinematics. fields.description:
For Spot/Pyramid Area Lights
The bulb's shape is pushed forward along the light direction by this many meters. The purpose is to allow the light to be recessed into the ceiling/wall so that its cone is roughly the size of the bulb when it emerges. Then this push forward attribute allows the bulb to appear where it's meant to be, not at the recessed location.

To support this, the cut on distance defines when lighting starts. The volume between the light's origin and this dead zone has no lighting. e.g. for a spot light, this would truncate the cone's tip. The transition between not-lit and lit is sharp and abrupt - there is no graceful fade-in.
